title: Cache Read/Write Patterns
summary: Cache-aside, read-through, write-through, and write-behind — the four ways an application and a cache can hand data back and forth, and what each one trades away.

slides.markdown:
Knowing that a cache exists (see [caching fundamentals](caching-fundamentals)) is only half the job — you also need a rule for *how* the application, the cache, and the database talk to each other on every read and write. That rule is a **caching pattern**.

The four common patterns — cache-aside, read-through, write-through, and write-behind — differ in who's responsible for populating the cache and how far behind the database the cache is allowed to fall. Picking the wrong one is a common way real systems either serve stale data or lose writes.

slides.sectionTitle: Cache-aside (lazy loading): the most common pattern
slides.markdown:
In **cache-aside** (also called lazy loading), the application talks to the cache and the database directly, and the cache only knows what the app has explicitly put into it. On a read: check the cache; on a miss, read the database, then write the result into the cache for next time. On a write: write to the database, and either update or delete the corresponding cache entry.

It's the default pattern for a reason — it's simple, and the cache only ever holds data that's actually been requested, so you never waste memory pre-loading things nobody asked for.

The cost: the *first* request for any given key always misses and pays full database latency, and the application owns the caching logic instead of it being hidden in a library.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: cache-aside read and write flow
slides.markdown:
![Cache-aside read path on a miss and write path](assets/cache-aside-flow.svg)

The read path has three steps on a miss: check cache, fall through to the database, then backfill the cache so the next reader gets a hit. The write path is shorter: write the database first, then invalidate (or update) the cache entry so a stale value isn't left behind.

Notice the app is in the loop on every step — cache-aside gives you full control at the cost of writing that logic yourself in every place data is read or written.

assets.alt: Cache-aside read path on a miss and write path

slides.sectionTitle: Read-through and write-through: pushing the logic into the cache layer
slides.markdown:
**Read-through** flips cache-aside's responsibility: instead of the app checking the cache and falling back to the database itself, the cache library is configured to know how to fetch from the database on a miss, so the app only ever talks to the cache. **Write-through** is the write-side equivalent — the app writes to the cache, and the cache synchronously writes that value through to the database before the write is considered done.

Together they centralize the caching logic in one place instead of scattering it across every call site, which is valuable when many parts of a codebase touch the same data.

The cost is coupling: the cache now needs to understand your data-loading logic, and a write-through write is only as fast as the slower of the cache write and the database write, since both must succeed.

slides.sectionTitle: Write-behind (write-back): async writes and the risk it takes on
slides.markdown:
**Write-behind** (or write-back) writes to the cache immediately and returns success to the caller right away — the write to the database happens later, asynchronously, often batched with other writes. This makes writes extremely fast from the caller's perspective, and batching many writes into fewer database round-trips reduces load on the database.

The trade is durability: between the cache write and the eventual database flush, that data exists only in the cache. If the cache crashes or the node is lost before the flush runs, that write is gone permanently — the database never saw it.

This pattern shows up in systems that can tolerate losing a few seconds of writes in a rare crash, in exchange for consistently low write latency — high-throughput counters and analytics pipelines are common users.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: all four patterns — consistency, latency, complexity
slides.markdown:
| Pattern | Write latency | Consistency risk | Who owns the logic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cache-aside | Fast (DB only) | Brief staleness until next read repopulates | Application |
| Read-through | Fast (DB only, on read) | Same as cache-aside, hidden in cache library | Cache library |
| Write-through | Slower (cache + DB, synchronous) | Cache and DB stay consistent immediately | Cache library |
| Write-behind | Fastest (cache only) | Data loss risk if cache crashes before flush | Cache library, async |

**How to decide:** default to cache-aside unless you have a specific reason not to — reach for write-through when the cache and database must never disagree, and write-behind only when raw write throughput matters more than the small risk of losing the last few writes.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: cache-aside read path in pseudocode
slides.markdown:
The core of cache-aside is one `if` branch on the read path:

```python
def get_user(user_id):
    value = cache.get(f"user:{user_id}")
    if value is not None:
        return value  # cache hit

    value = db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s", user_id)
    cache.set(f"user:{user_id}", value, ttl_seconds=300)
    return value
```

On a hit, the database is never touched. On a miss, the database is queried once and the result is stored with a TTL, so the *next* request for this user is a hit. Note the `ttl_seconds=300` — a bounded expiry is a cheap safety net even alongside explicit invalidation, in case an invalidation is ever missed.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: write-behind losing data on a cache crash before flush
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Write-behind is strictly better than write-through — it's faster with no real downside."

**Why it's wrong:** write-behind's speed comes directly from telling the caller "done" before the database has the data. If the cache node crashes, restarts, or loses power before the queued write flushes, that data is gone — the database will never see it, and there's no way to recover it after the fact.

**Correct model:** write-behind trades durability for speed; only use it for data where losing the last few seconds of writes in a rare crash is an acceptable cost (like a view counter), never for data that must survive — payments, orders, anything a user would notice missing.
